summary: Alexander Eggers (1864–1937) was a linguist and Indologist who earned his Ph.D. at the University of Tartu (1885–1894), studying under Leo Meyer and Leopold von Schroeder. He later served at Tallinn Cathedral School and directed the Privatlyzeum Greifswald.

Alexander Faulkner (d. 1881) worked in Indology and other fields. He served in the Indian Civil Service beginning in 1839 and was an Assistant Commissioner in the Customs, Salt, and Opium Department until 1874.
Alexander Freiman studied under Fyodor Shcherbatskoy around 1903–1907 and under Christian Bartholomae around 1906–1908.

Tibetologist and Buddhist studies scholar Alexander Gardner studied at Kalamazoo College, Michigan State University, and earned a Ph.D. from the University of Michigan under Donald S. Lopez Jr. He held a post at the Buddhist Digital Resource Center.

Alexander Hamilton (1762–1824) was an Indologist who served as Professor of Sanskrit and Hindu Literature at East India Company College (1806–1818). He founded the Royal Asiatic Society in 1823 and taught scholars including Franz Bopp and Friedrich Schlegel.
Alexander Henderson Diack (1862–1929) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the University of Aberdeen from 1876 to 1879 and at King's College, Cambridge, from 1879 to 1881.
Alexander James O'Neill is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Japanology who pursued PhD candidacy at the University of Toronto and held a post as a research fellow at Taisho University.

Alexander Johnston (1775–1849) studied under Christian Friedrich Schwartz and at Göttingen and Lincoln's Inn. He served as Chief Justice and Council member in Ceylon, worked in Indology and history/archaeology, and founded the Royal Asiatic Society in 1823.

Alexander Kabanoff (1952–2003) specialized in Japanology and Buddhist studies. Attested in 2000, he was a Senior Researcher at Saint Petersburg State University and head of the Japanese section at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

Alexander Kasimovich Kazembek (1802–1870) was a scholar of linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and history/archaeology. He held academic posts at Kazan Imperial University (~1826–1849) and Imperial St. Petersburg University (~1849–1870).

Alexander Kingsbury Smith studied at American University, Oxford, and EPHE (PhD 2011–2016). Specializing in Tibetology and Buddhist studies, he taught at EPHE and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg, worked at Otani University, and directed Armchair Academics and Ligature Historical Filmwerke.

Alexander Kinloch Forbes (1821–1865), an Indologist and historian, studied at East India Company College and under Dalpatram. He founded the Gujarat Vernacular Society (1848) and Forbes Gujarati Sabha (1865), and served as Vice-Chancellor of the University of Mumbai (1862).

Alexander Lubotsky is a linguist and Indologist who studied at Moscow State University and earned his BA and PhD at Leiden University under Robert S. P. Beekes. In 1999, he became professor of Comparative Indo-European Linguistics at Leiden.
Alexander Macmillan worked in religious studies and Buddhist studies, studying at the SIT Graduate Institute under advisor Elizabeth Morrison (attested 2013).

Alexander Meyrick Broadley (1847–1916) was an Indology and history/archaeology scholar who studied law at Lincoln's Inn (~1866–1869). He served as an Assistant and Collector in the Indian Civil Service from 1869 to 1872.
Alexander Murray (1775–1813) was a linguist and Indologist who studied at the University of Edinburgh (~1794–1812), where he became Professor of Oriental Languages in 1812.

Alexander O. Hsu is a scholar of religious and Buddhist studies who earned his PhD from the University of Chicago under Paul Copp and Christian K. Wedemeyer (~2011–2018). He held a teaching position at North Dakota State University.

Alexander Piatigorsky (1929–2009) was an Indologist and Buddhist studies philosopher who studied at Moscow State University. He worked at the Institute of Oriental Studies and later served as Professor of the Ancient History of South Asia at SOAS (1990–2001).

Alexander Potebnja (1835–1891) was a linguist and philosopher who earned his PhD at the University of Kharkiv and studied under Albrecht Weber. He served as a professor at Kharkiv (~1862–1891) and was an Associate member of the Saint Petersburg Academy.

Alexander Rea (1858–1924) was an Indologist and archaeologist who spent his career at the Archaeological Survey of India, serving as Assistant in 1882, head in 1886, and Superintendent from 1902 to 1913.
